html:
Have you ever thought about the home you grew up in – really thought about it – as a place that shaped who you are today? Have you thought about the bedroom that you shared with your sibling, and what that taught you about sharing; or the fact that you had your own room, and what that taught you about personal space? Have you considered how tidy it was and whether you mirror that in your home today, or who took care of the space, which photos were on the walls, how the lounge was set up – all of which may have taught you lessons about how to live?

Your home had its rules and conventions, and it’s likely that you’ve carried many of them with you. Some rules of the home are explicit (‘Clean up your space before bedtime’), and many are implicit (leaving the toilet seat up/down). Rules about what is acceptable, respectable, comfortable, tasteful or hygienic operate all around the home. This is sometimes easier to notice when in other people’s homes, especially if you see something you’d never tolerate in your own (eg, the cat sprawled across the kitchen table, or everyone wearing outdoor shoes indoors).

Of course, the rules of other homes are entirely natural to those who live there. In my work as a business anthropologist, I’ve hung out in people’s homes in more than 20 countries. Most of the time I’m doing it as part of a research project with a paying client (including companies like IKEA), but the point is rarely whether people use a specific product or not. It’s really about how they live.

In many of the Chinese homes that my team and I have visited, when people arrive home, they immediately change into indoor clothes and slippers, creating a psychological, physical and hygienic boundary between outside and inside spheres.

In many homes in the United Kingdom, where I grew up, guests are offered tea within minutes, and the tea gives the (often conversationally awkward) Brits time to acclimatise to one another.

In some Saudi Arabian homes, guest reception areas are carefully arranged to signal hospitality, dignity and family honour. And in the female side of the house, there’s play, connection, and messy bedrooms.

Each home you visit says, in its own way: this is how life should be lived.

A home can, of course, tell you an enormous amount about who the inhabitants are as individuals. Imagine you’re allowed to walk around someone’s house when they aren’t there. Think about how much you could learn just from the way they set up the home: which books are displayed prominently, and which are hidden (non-fiction vs ‘trashy’ novels); whether family photos are recent or old, formal or casual, or entirely absent; the focal point in each room (a TV, dining table, toys, artwork?); whether the living room is designed for guests, children, solitude or escape. Our homes are biographies made physical.

But as the Chinese, British and Saudi examples suggest, these physical biographies are, in part, descriptions of the communities we live in. Our homes reflect various shared living practices, and these are often much more uniform within a culture than we might realise.

Collectivist values play out in multigenerational homes throughout Shanghai and Beijing

The home, then, is also a form of cultural infrastructure: it provides what’s ‘normal’ for a range of life’s activities, such as eating, sleeping, socialising, play, cleaning, work, negotiating and much more. You can see this clearly in the physical organisation and sharing of space within homes. In Polish homes that I’ve visited, for example, I have found that it’s hard to figure out which room is a bedroom, as most low- to middle-income households sleep on sofa beds that they pull out and put away the next morning. Communist undertones still feature in the design of the buildings, where function was prioritised over form. A family apartment might have only one or two bedrooms because the assumption is that siblings can share, that grandparents can take the main bedroom while the parents sleep in the living room. Underlying these design principles is the idea that space is shared, rather than owned.

In France, life at home commonly centres around the dining-room table, a place imbued with ritual every morning and evening. Given the amount of time spent there, it inevitably becomes the place where taste, manners and the art of polite conversation are taught and passed through generations. I’ve often pondered why French children seem so well behaved at the table compared with children in England, where I grew up. It seems to me that French children often enjoy being at the table because the adults involve them in the discussions, whereas in England the conversations often happen between the adults while the children are expected to watch (which tends to result in boredom and playing up).

Returning to China, we see collectivist values play out in multigenerational homes throughout Shanghai and Beijing. Often, the grandparents come to live with the parents and grandchildren so that the parents can return to work. In Shanghai, survey data suggest as many as 90 per cent of children under the age of three have a grandparent who takes part in childcare every week. When talking to Chinese parents, I quickly realised that they didn’t necessarily like their in-laws any more than people do in other parts of the world, it’s just that they accept that this is what happens in their culture. What’s more, the housing in China’s first-tier cities doesn’t always cater well for all three generations, adding to the level of cooperation and compromise that families must go through when living together.

In these and other cultures, there are naturally still people who rebel and go against the cultural rules, including the ones they learn at home. Culture is flexible and allows for that. But the rebellion exists only because rules exist in the first place.

Does a messy space indicate laziness, or creativity? Does quiet mean respect, or emotional distance?

‘Well, my home is different from other people’s,’ you might say. Yes, of course it is: it reflects your personal taste and experiences, whether through travel souvenirs, prayer objects, sports memorabilia, or that old chair that nobody dares throw away. But even when it comes to aesthetics, there are cultural patterns. In an American teenager’s bedroom, a framed poster of the New York City skyline might reflect their aspiration or sense of identity. A family’s religious calligraphy in Riyadh may express their faith and moral grounding. Antique furniture in London could suggest continuity and class taste. In a Danish home, flags might appear during celebrations to symbolise shared civic identity.

Homes are also places where communal relationships are organised in keeping with cultural norms. Some households are porous: neighbours wander in, cousins stay over, doors are left unlocked (I’ve noted this sort of porosity a lot in Poland and India). Other homes are tightly bounded: visits arranged in advance, private rooms respected, front doors acting like borders (frequently the case in the UK or the United States). Other variations matter, such as whether it’s an urban or rural environment, or a wealthy or poor neighbourhood – but national cultural characteristics drive these differences as well.

Children learn these rules long before they can explain them, based on behaviours that could have wildly different connotations from place to place. Does a messy space indicate laziness, or creativity? Does quiet mean respect, or emotional distance? Are bedrooms private, or communal territory? Do unexpected guests bring joy, or disruption? Is food seen more as fuel, or an expression of love? Children learn the rules of life from what’s normal at home, and these rules are reflected in how people organise and structure the home around them.

Cultural changes often appear in homes before they appear in headlines. The cost-of-living crisis has encouraged more shared living in London and New York, an increase in multigenerational homes across Europe, smaller private spaces in China and South Korea, and a thriving second-hand market across the world. It’s also led to pride in the ‘tiny home’ movement, and an increase in learning crafts like upholstery and upcycling. Generational changes are visible too. Many younger adults are less interested in the ‘show home’ ideal of previous decades. Perfection can seem expensive and suspiciously performative. For many younger people, authenticity, flexibility and emotional comfort may matter more than matching cushions. The home keeps changing because culture keeps changing, and when the culture changes, so too do the rules that we live by. Moving to a tiny home – or just a smaller one – might be a response to economic conditions, but it also teaches people new ways of living.

The phrase ‘Make yourself at home’ is usually read as an invitation. It can also be read as an instruction. Home is one of the most important places that shape who we are and how we live. And this is why visiting someone else’s home can feel so revealing, especially when that person comes from a culture that’s different from yours. By stepping through the doorway, you might be stepping into another cultural universe. When you notice the shoes by the door, the untouched ‘good room’, or the Lego bricks scattered across the floor, ask yourself: whose rules am I looking at?
